title: The Truth About the Organic Label (What USDA Organic Actually Means)
summary: Rapid-fire explainer on what the USDA organic seal covers and what it does not, the evidence on residues, omega-3s and health, environmental trade-offs, import fraud risk, and where the premium is worth paying.

assertions.quote: Organic food carries a 20 to 100% price premium in a $61 billion US market.
An organic cookie is still a cookie. The seal certifies farming, not the finished product's healthiness.
the word natural has no legal definition at all, making it essentially meaningless.
There are four organic tiers and only 95% or higher earns the front of pack seal.
Made with organic is the third tier and can legally contain 30% non-organic ingredients.
Farms must practice organic methods for three full years before crops can legally be sold as organic.

verdicts.note: 7 CFR 205.202(b) requires that no prohibited substance was applied to the field for 3 years before harvest of a crop sold as organic.
ERS cites the 3-year transition period required to convert nonorganic pastureland to organic as a brake on organic dairy herd growth.

assertions.quote: Later research found organic dairy and meat do contain higher levels of omega-3 fatty acids.

verdicts.note: 2016 meta-analyses found roughly half again as much omega-3 in organic milk and meat, driven by more grazing.

assertions.quote: That omega-3 boost seems driven by grass-feeding practices more common on organic farms, not certification itself.

verdicts.note: The meta-analysis authors attributed the difference to grazing and forage intake, which conventional grass-fed systems can match.

assertions.quote: European studies consistently find higher insect, bird, and plant diversity on organic farmland.
Organic farming needs 20 to 25% more land to grow the same amount of food.
Domestic organic with short supply chains carries far lower fraud risk than imported organic goods.
